old: It provided not only that, in case Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., L.L.D., F.R.S., etc., should die, all his possessions were to pass to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde,” but also that in case of Dr. Jekyll’s “disappearance or unexplained absence for any period exceeding three calendar months,” the said Edward Hyde should step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes without further delay, free of any burden or obligation beyond paying a few small sums to the doctor’s household.
new: It provided that if Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., LL.D., F.R.S., etc., should die, everything he owned would pass to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde.” But it went further: if Dr. Jekyll should “disappear or be unaccountably absent for any period exceeding three calendar months,” Edward Hyde was to step straight into his place, with no further delay, and no burden beyond a few small payments to the doctor’s household.
reason: This single sentence carries the whole premise the reader needs to track for the rest of the book (Hyde inherits on Jekyll's death OR disappearance), but it's delivered as one long legal-document sentence with 'not only...but also', a parenthetical string of degree abbreviations, and repeated legalese ('the said Edward Hyde...the said Henry Jekyll's shoes'). Heard once, aloud, a first-time listener is very likely to lose exactly which condition triggers Hyde's inheritance, which weakens the mystery Utterson spends the rest of the book worrying about.

old: He might see a reason for his friend’s strange preference or bondage (call it which you please), and even for the startling clauses of the will
new: He might see a reason for his friend’s strange attachment to Hyde — call it a fondness, or a hold Hyde had over him — and even for the startling clauses of the will
reason: 'Bondage' is used here in its older sense of a binding obligation/attachment, but to a contemporary reader or listener the word now reads first as slavery or restraint (or its sexual sense), which is a jarring, momentarily confusing association in a sentence that isn't about either. Not a blocker since the parenthetical softens it, but worth swapping for a word without the modern baggage.

old: It seems she had a romantic streak, for she sat down on her trunk
new: It seems she had a dreamy, fanciful streak, for she sat down on her trunk
reason: 'Romantic' here means fanciful/sentimental (in keeping with 'fell into a daydream'), but the modern default reading of 'romantic' is love-related, and nothing romantic in that sense follows. A brief but avoidable stumble for a listener expecting the sentence to be about romance.

old: Profound a double-dealer as I was, I was never in any sense a hypocrite
new: As profound a double-dealer as I was, I was never in any sense a hypocrite
reason: This is an inverted 'as...as' construction with the leading 'as' dropped, an old-fashioned literary pattern ('Great a fool as he was...'). Read aloud cold, 'Profound a double-dealer as I was' parses awkwardly on first hearing — a listener may need a beat to realize it isn't a sentence fragment. Restoring the leading 'As' makes the construction immediately legible without changing the meaning or register.

old: Men have hired hitmen before now to carry out their crimes
new: Men have hired ruffians before now to carry out their crimes
reason: 'Hitmen' is a 20th-century American slang term (mob/gangster register) dropped into Jekyll's otherwise formal, reflective Victorian-modernized voice. It's perfectly easy to understand, but it's a register mismatch that stands out against the surrounding sentence and the rest of the confession's diction — the only place in the book slang this modern appears.
